questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a cistern in 12 hours and pipe B can fill it in 8 hours. If both pipes are opened simultaneously, how long will the cistern take to be completely filled?

options.option_text: 3 hours 36 minutes
4 hours 48 minutes
5 hours 20 minutes
6 hours 10 minutes

questions.explanation: A's rate = 1/12 per hour; B's rate = 1/8 per hour. Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/8 = 2/24 + 3/24 = 5/24 per hour. Time = 24/5 = 4.8 hours = 4 hours 48 minutes.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours while pipe B drains the full tank in 4 hours. If both pipes are opened together when the tank is completely full, how long will the tank take to become empty?

options.option_text: 10 hours
8 hours
12 hours
24 hours

questions.explanation: A fills at 1/6 per hour; B drains at 1/4 per hour. Net drain rate = 1/4 − 1/6 = 3/12 − 2/12 = 1/12 per hour. A full tank empties in 1 ÷ (1/12) = 12 hours.

questions.stem: Pipes A, B, and C can individually fill a tank in 6, 9, and 12 hours respectively. If all three pipes are opened simultaneously, how long will the tank take to be completely filled?

options.option_text: 3 hours 0 minutes
2 hours 15 minutes
4 hours 20 minutes
2 hours 46 minutes

questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/9 + 1/12 = 6/36 + 4/36 + 3/36 = 13/36 per hour. Time = 36/13 ≈ 2.77 hours ≈ 2 hours 46 minutes. Verify: 13/36 × 36/13 = 1 (full tank). ✓

questions.stem: Two inlet pipes A and B can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. An outlet pipe C can drain the full tank in 20 hours. If all three pipes are opened together, in how much time will the tank be filled?

options.option_text: 8 hours 34 minutes
7 hours 30 minutes
10 hours 0 minutes
6 hours 40 minutes

questions.explanation: Net fill rate = 1/10 + 1/15 − 1/20 = 6/60 + 4/60 − 3/60 = 7/60 per hour. Time = 60/7 ≈ 8.57 hours ≈ 8 hours 34 minutes. Verify: 7/60 × 60/7 = 1. ✓

questions.stem: A pipe fills a tank in 20 hours. Due to a leak at the bottom, the tank actually takes 60 hours to fill completely. How long would the leak alone take to empty a full tank?

options.option_text: 40 hours
20 hours
30 hours
12 hours

questions.explanation: Fill rate = 1/20 per hour. Net rate with leak = 1/60 per hour. Leak rate = 1/20 − 1/60 = 3/60 − 1/60 = 2/60 = 1/30 per hour. Leak alone empties a full tank in 30 hours.

questions.stem: Pipe A alone fills 1/3 of a tank in 5 hours. Pipes A and B together can fill the full tank in 6 hours. A worked alone for the first 5 hours, after which B also joined. Find the total time taken to fill the tank completely.

options.option_text: 8 hours
9 hours
10 hours
7 hours

questions.explanation: A's rate = (1/3) ÷ 5 = 1/15 per hour. A+B combined rate = 1/6 per hour. After 5 hours, A fills 5 × (1/15) = 1/3; remaining = 2/3. Time for A+B to fill the rest = (2/3) ÷ (1/6) = (2/3) × 6 = 4 hours. Total = 5 + 4 = 9 hours.

questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B can fill it in 18 hours. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with A. How long will it take for the tank to be completely filled?

options.option_text: 15 hours 00 minutes
14 hours 00 minutes
13 hours 40 minutes
14 hours 20 minutes

questions.explanation: Per 2-hour cycle: A fills 1/12, B fills 1/18; combined = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36. After 7 complete cycles (14 hours): 7 × 5/36 = 35/36 filled. Remaining = 1/36. A's turn next: time = (1/36) ÷ (1/12) = 12/36 = 1/3 hour = 20 minutes. Total = 14 hours 20 minutes.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank at exactly twice the rate of Pipe B. When both pipes work together, they fill the tank in 10 hours. How long does Pipe B alone take to fill the same tank?

options.option_text: 15 hours to fill the full tank
20 hours to fill the full tank
25 hours to fill the full tank
30 hours to fill the full tank

questions.explanation: Let Pipe B's rate = 1/b per hour. Then Pipe A's rate = 2/b. Together: 3/b = 1/10, so b = 30. Pipe B alone takes 30 hours. The very common trap is 15 hours, which is actually Pipe A's time (30/2). Choosing 20 hours comes from simply doubling the combined time of 10 hours, ignoring the rate relationship entirely.

questions.stem: A completely full water tank has two drainage pipes P and Q. Pipe P alone empties the full tank in 18 hours and Pipe Q alone in 9 hours. If both outlets are opened simultaneously, in how many hours will the tank be completely empty?

options.option_text: 4 hours 30 minutes to empty the tank
6 hours to completely drain the tank
9 hours to completely drain the tank
12 hours to completely drain the tank

questions.explanation: Combined drain rate = 1/18 + 1/9 = 1/18 + 2/18 = 3/18 = 1/6 per hour, so the tank empties in 6 hours. The most common distractor is 9 hours — that is Q's time alone, ignoring P's contribution. The 4.5-hour trap arises from halving Q's solo time without any justification.

questions.stem: A pipe fills a cistern in 24 hours. After running for 8 hours, a crack develops at the bottom that would drain the full cistern in 36 hours on its own. How many additional hours are needed after the crack appears for the cistern to become completely full?

options.option_text: 32 hours more to completely fill the cistern
36 hours more to completely fill the cistern
40 hours more to completely fill the cistern
48 hours more to completely fill the cistern

questions.explanation: After 8 hours, 8/24 = 1/3 is filled; remaining = 2/3. With the crack open, net fill rate = 1/24 − 1/36 = 3/72 − 2/72 = 1/72 per hour. Time for remaining 2/3: (2/3) ÷ (1/72) = 48 hours. The trap of 36 hours comes from confusing the crack's own drain time with the additional time needed to complete filling.

questions.stem: Pipes A and B together fill a tank in 12 hours; Pipes B and C together fill the same tank in 15 hours. Pipe A is twice as efficient as Pipe C. How long does Pipe A alone take to fill the tank?

options.option_text: 20 hours to fill the tank alone
24 hours to fill the tank alone
30 hours to fill the tank alone
36 hours to fill the tank alone

questions.explanation: A+B = 1/12 and B+C = 1/15, so A − C = 1/12 − 1/15 = 5/60 − 4/60 = 1/60. Since A = 2C, substituting gives C = 1/60 (takes 60 hours alone) and A = 2/60 = 1/30, so A alone takes 30 hours. The 20-hour trap comes from ignoring the A = 2C condition and guessing based on LCM shortcuts.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 20 hours and Pipe B in 30 hours. Both pipes are opened together at time zero. After how many hours should Pipe B be closed so that the tank is exactly full at the 15-hour mark?

options.option_text: After 5 hours, pipe B must be shut off
After 6 hours, pipe B must be shut off
After 7.5 hours, pipe B must be shut off
After 10 hours, pipe B must be shut off

questions.explanation: Let B run for t hours. Work equation: t(1/20 + 1/30) + (15 − t)(1/20) = 1 → t(5/60) + (15 − t)(3/60) = 1 → 5t + 45 − 3t = 60 → 2t = 15 → t = 7.5 hours. The 10-hour trap comes from setting up the equation incorrectly, forgetting that A continues working alone after B closes.

questions.stem: Pipe X fills a tank in 12 hours. A small leak at the bottom causes the tank to fill in 16 hours instead. Pipe Y alone fills the same tank in 8 hours. If only Pipe Y and the leak are active (Pipe X is shut), how long does it take to fill the tank?

options.option_text: 8 hours 48 minutes to fill the tank
9 hours 36 minutes to fill the tank
9 hours 12 minutes to fill the tank
10 hours 24 minutes to fill the tank

questions.explanation: First isolate the leak: with X open, fill rate = 1/16; X alone = 1/12; so leak rate = 1/12 − 1/16 = 4/48 − 3/48 = 1/48 per hour (drains in 48 hours). Now Y + leak: 1/8 − 1/48 = 6/48 − 1/48 = 5/48 per hour. Time = 48/5 = 9.6 hours = 9 hours 36 minutes. The 10 hours 24 minutes trap arises from wrongly using 1/16 as the leak's drain rate rather than computing it as the difference.

questions.stem: Pipes A, B, and C fill a tank in 20, 25, and 60 hours respectively. They open in strict rotation — Pipe A for 1 hour, then Pipe B for 1 hour, then Pipe C for 1 hour — and this 3-hour cycle repeats. At exactly what point does the tank first become completely full, and during which pipe's turn does it happen?

options.option_text: 27 hours 48 minutes, during Pipe A's turn
27 hours 20 minutes, during Pipe B's turn
28 hours 00 minutes, at Pipe C's turn end
29 hours 36 minutes, during Pipe C's turn

questions.explanation: Each 3-hour cycle fills 1/20 + 1/25 + 1/60 = 15/300 + 12/300 + 5/300 = 32/300 = 8/75. After 9 complete cycles (27 hours): 9 × 8/75 = 72/75 = 24/25 full; remaining = 1/25. In the 10th cycle, Pipe A opens first at rate 1/20. Time to fill 1/25: (1/25) ÷ (1/20) = 20/25 = 4/5 hour = 48 minutes. Tank fills at 27 h 48 min during A's turn. Choosing Pipe B's turn is the distractor for candidates who misjudge that 1/25 > 1/20 and assume A's slot is insufficient.
